title: Meta Ordered to Pay New Mexico $25 Billion for Deceiving Users About Privacy on Facebook
description: A New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for intentionally deceiving Facebook users about privacy controls, marking the largest fine against the company. The ruling found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws related to misleading statements about user data handling. This case stems from the Cambridge Analytica scandal where Facebook data was harvested for political advertising. Meta disputes the ruling and plans to appeal. The fine significantly exceeds previous penalties, including a $5 billion FTC fine in 2019. The judgment aims to hold tech companies accountable for privacy misrepresentations.
aiSummary: A New Mexico jury found Meta liable for intentionally deceiving Facebook users about privacy controls, resulting in a $25 billion fine. The court ruled that Facebook falsely promised users control over their data, violating state consumer protection laws over 43 million times. The case relates to the 2016 Cambridge Analytica data harvesting incident. Meta argues the state failed to prove harm and plans to appeal. The ruling is notable for its size, surpassing prior fines against Meta, including a $5 billion FTC penalty. The fine is intended as a strong message to tech companies about accountability for privacy practices.
aiImpact: The ruling imposes a $25 billion financial penalty on Meta, the largest ever against the company, for deceptive privacy practices affecting millions of users in New Mexico. It highlights legal risks for tech companies regarding user data privacy and transparency. The judgment may influence regulatory and legal approaches to privacy enforcement. Meta's business operations in New Mexico could be impacted, though the company plans to appeal. The case underscores ongoing scrutiny of social media platforms' handling of personal data and user trust.
